goals: Explain how the drain of wealth, the ruin of crafts and peasant distress fed nationalism

Explain how the Press spread political awareness

slides.heading: Why did Indians begin to feel like one nation?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **economic exploitation**, **repressive policies** and the **Press**.

nodes.label: Ruin of crafts and peasant distress

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the drain of wealth, the ruin of crafts and peasant distress, Lord Lytton's measures, the Ilbert Bill controversy and the role of the Press
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In the second half of the nineteenth century, people in Bengal, Bombay, Madras and Punjab began to think of themselves as Indians with common interests. Why? In this part we look at three streams: economic hardship under colonial rule, laws that treated Indians unequally, and newspapers that carried these grievances to readers across the country.

slides.heading: Four streams, one feeling
slides.body_md: Exploitation, repression, reform and the Press all fed **national feeling**.

visual.caption: Four streams that fed one national feeling.

slides.narration: This hub diagram shows four streams that flowed into Indian nationalism. Economic exploitation and repressive policies created grievances. Reform movements gave Indians self-respect and unity. The Press carried ideas to readers everywhere. In this part we study exploitation, repression and the Press; reform comes in Part 2.

slides.heading: The drain of wealth
slides.body_md: Wealth flowed to **Britain** without an equal return, as **Dadabhai Naoroji** argued.

nodes.label: Salaries and pensions of British officials
Home charges and interest on loans
Wealth reaches Britain without equal return

visual.alt: Flow of the drain of wealth: Indian revenues and trade pay for salaries and pensions of British officials, home charges and interest on loans, and profits of British firms, so wealth reaches Britain without an equal return
visual.caption: The drain, as the early nationalists described it.

slides.narration: Early nationalists, led by Dadabhai Naoroji, argued that India's wealth was being drained to Britain. Salaries and pensions of British officials, charges paid in London, interest on loans and the profits of British firms all left the country. Nothing equal came back. This argument turned poverty from a matter of fate into a criticism of colonial rule.

slides.heading: Ruin of handicrafts
slides.body_md: Cheap **machine-made** goods and one-sided duties destroyed **artisan** livelihoods.

rows: Cheap machine-made British cloth enters India
Local weavers cannot match the price
Indian goods face high duties in Britain
Courts and nobles who bought fine crafts decline
Home demand for luxury goods falls
Artisans move to farming as labourers
More pressure on land and more poverty

visual.alt: Table of changes and their effects on artisans: cheap British machine cloth undercuts weavers, Indian goods face high duties in Britain, old patrons decline, and artisans move to farm labour, adding pressure on land
visual.caption: Imagined classroom summary of a well-known trend.

slides.narration: India had been famous for fine cloth. In the nineteenth century, cheap machine-made cloth from British factories entered Indian markets, while Indian goods faced high duties in Britain. Old patrons such as royal courts declined. Many weavers and other artisans lost their work and became farm labourers. Nationalists pointed to this as proof that colonial rule served British interests.

slides.heading: Peasants and famines
slides.body_md: Heavy **land revenue**, **debt** and slow **famine relief**.

nodes.label: Payment due even in bad seasons
Loans from moneylenders at high interest
Famine relief seen as too little

visual.alt: Flow of peasant distress: heavy land revenue due even in bad seasons leads to loans at high interest, loss of land and poverty, and famine relief is seen as too little
visual.caption: Why villages grew restless.

slides.narration: Peasants paid a heavy land revenue, and it fell due even when the rains failed. To pay it, many borrowed from moneylenders at high interest and slowly lost their land. During the great famine of eighteen seventy-six to seventy-eight, relief was widely seen as too little and too late. Rural distress became one more grievance against the government.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: sorting grievances
slides.body_md: Is each imagined grievance **economic** or caused by a **repressive law**?
bullets: Step 1: does it concern **livelihood, money or land**? Economic.
Step 2: does a **law** treat Indians **unequally** or silence them? Repressive.
Step 3: name the law where you can.

rows: A weaver's looms stand idle because mill cloth is cheaper
A teacher must apply for a licence to keep a gun his European neighbour keeps freely
A Marathi weekly is warned for criticising famine relief
A farmer borrows to pay revenue after a failed monsoon

visual.alt: Worked example table sorting four imagined grievances: idle looms and a farmer borrowing for revenue are economic; a licence for a gun and a warned Marathi weekly are repressive measures
visual.caption: Ask: is the cause about money and livelihood, or about a law that treats Indians unequally?

slides.narration: Let us sort four imagined grievances. A weaver whose looms stand idle because mill cloth is cheaper has an economic grievance. A farmer who borrows to pay revenue after a failed monsoon also has an economic one. A teacher who needs a licence for a gun that his European neighbour keeps freely faces the Arms Act. A Marathi weekly warned for criticising famine relief faces the Press Act.

slides.heading: Lord Lytton's measures
slides.body_md: The **Durbar (1877)**, the **Vernacular Press Act (1878)** and the **Arms Act (1878)**.

rows: Delhi Durbar to proclaim the Queen Empress of India
Lavish spending during a severe famine
Curbed Indian-language papers; English papers left free
Licence needed by Indians; Europeans exempt

visual.alt: Table of Lord Lytton's measures: the Delhi Durbar of 1877 during a famine, the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 that curbed Indian-language papers only, and the Arms Act of 1878 that required Indians but not Europeans to hold licences

slides.narration: Lord Lytton was Viceroy from eighteen seventy-six to eighteen eighty. In eighteen seventy-seven he held a grand Durbar in Delhi to proclaim Queen Victoria Empress of India, while millions suffered in a famine. In eighteen seventy-eight came the Vernacular Press Act, which curbed newspapers in Indian languages, and the Arms Act, which required Indians but not Europeans to hold licences for arms.

slides.heading: Quick check: who introduced the Bill?
slides.body_md: True or false: the Ilbert Bill was introduced under Lord Ripon.
slides.narration: Lytton was followed by a different viceroy. Was the Ilbert Bill introduced in his time?

slides.heading: The Ilbert Bill controversy, 1883
slides.body_md: A Bill to let **Indian judges** try **Europeans** met fierce European protest.

nodes.label: 1883: Bill lets Indian judges try Europeans
Government gives way and dilutes the Bill
Indians learn the value of organised protest

visual.alt: Flow of the Ilbert Bill controversy: in 1883 a Bill to let Indian judges try Europeans meets loud European protest, the government dilutes it, and Indians see racial prejudice and learn the value of organised protest
visual.caption: Under Lord Ripon, 1883.

slides.narration: Under Lord Ripon, the Ilbert Bill of eighteen eighty-three proposed that qualified Indian judges could try Europeans in criminal cases. Many Europeans in India protested loudly, and the government gave way and diluted the Bill. Indians saw the racial prejudice behind the protest. They also learnt that organised, united agitation could change government policy, a lesson they soon applied themselves.

slides.heading: Why these measures mattered
columns:
**What Indians felt**

- Racial **inequality** in law
- Their **voice** being silenced
- **Indifference** to famine

**What Indians learnt**

- Grievances were **common** to all regions
- **Organised protest** could work
- An **all-India body** was needed

rows: Delhi Durbar to proclaim the Queen Empress of India
Lavish spending during a severe famine
Curbed Indian-language papers; English papers left free
Licence needed by Indians; Europeans exempt

visual.alt: Table of Lord Lytton's measures: the Delhi Durbar of 1877 during a famine, the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 that curbed Indian-language papers only, and the Arms Act of 1878 that required Indians but not Europeans to hold licences

slides.narration: Look at these measures in two ways. Indians felt that the law treated them as unequal, that their newspapers were being silenced and that their suffering in famine was ignored. They also learnt something. These grievances were shared across every region, and the Ilbert Bill showed that organised protest could succeed. Both feelings pointed towards a national organisation.

slides.heading: The nationalist Press
slides.body_md: Newspapers in **English** and **Indian languages** carried news and criticism far and wide.

visual.alt: Table of four nationalist newspapers: Amrita Bazar Patrika of Calcutta, Bengali and then English from 1878; The Hindu of Madras, founded in 1878; Kesari in Marathi linked with Tilak; and The Bengalee linked with Surendranath Banerjee

slides.narration: The second half of the nineteenth century saw a growth of nationalist newspapers. Amrita Bazar Patrika of Calcutta, The Hindu of Madras, Kesari in Marathi linked with Bal Gangadhar Tilak, and The Bengalee of Surendranath Banerjee are four examples. They reported government policies, criticised injustice and published the views of Indian leaders.

slides.heading: Quick check: why Indian languages?
slides.body_md: Why did newspapers in Indian languages matter so much?
slides.narration: Only a small number of Indians could read English. What did Indian-language papers add?

slides.heading: How the Press built opinion
slides.body_md: Report, **criticise**, carry ideas, **link regions**.

visual.alt: Flow of the Press's role: reporting events, criticising unjust measures, carrying leaders' ideas and linking readers across regions build a shared national opinion
visual.caption: How newspapers built opinion.

slides.narration: The Press worked in several ways at once. It reported events and policies. It criticised measures such as the Press Act and the Durbar. It carried the speeches and writings of leaders to people who never met them. Most important, a reader in Madras could learn about a grievance in Punjab, so people began to see their problems as shared.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a 10-mark answer in three parts
slides.body_md: Plan for: Press Act **[3]**, Arms Act **[3]**, Ilbert Bill and nationalism **[4]**.
bullets: Part (i): what the Act did **plus** why Indians objected: three clear points.
Part (ii): the rule, who was exempt, the effect on opinion.
Part (iii): the proposal, the protest, the outcome, and **two** lessons for nationalism.
Use the dates **1878** and **1883**, and name **Lytton** and **Ripon**.

slides.narration: Here is how to plan a ten-mark question on repressive measures. Give three clear points for the Press Act: what it did, whom it spared and why Indians objected. Do the same for the Arms Act. For the four-mark part on the Ilbert Bill, state the proposal, the European protest, the outcome, and two lessons Indians drew. Dates and the names of viceroys earn easy marks.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: **Drain of wealth** (Naoroji), **ruin of crafts**, **peasant debt** and **famine**.
**Lytton:** Durbar 1877, Vernacular Press Act 1878, Arms Act 1878.
**Ilbert Bill 1883** (Ripon): racial prejudice exposed; lesson of organised protest.
**Press:** Amrita Bazar Patrika, The Hindu, Kesari, The Bengalee spread awareness.

nodes.label: Lytton's Durbar, Press Act and Arms Act
Ilbert Bill: lesson of organised protest

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: the drain and ruin of crafts, peasant debt and famine, Lytton's Durbar, Press Act and Arms Act, the Ilbert Bill as a lesson in organised protest, and the Press spreading the message
visual.caption: Part 1 in five lines.

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. The drain of wealth, the ruin of crafts and peasant distress made Indians question colonial rule. Lord Lytton's Durbar, Press Act and Arms Act added a sense of humiliation. The Ilbert Bill exposed racial prejudice and showed the power of organised protest. And the Press carried all of this to readers across India.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Write **1878** for both the Press Act and the Arms Act; the Durbar was **1877**.
The Press Act hit **Indian-language** papers only; say so.
The Ilbert Bill: **1883**, **Ripon**, Indian judges trying **Europeans**.
For "factors of nationalism", link each factor to **how** it changed Indian feeling.
slides.narration: Some tips. Remember eighteen seventy-eight for both Acts and eighteen seventy-seven for the Durbar. Say clearly that the Press Act targeted Indian-language newspapers. For the Ilbert Bill, write eighteen eighty-three, Lord Ripon, and Indian judges trying Europeans. And when you list factors of nationalism, always explain how each one changed what Indians felt.

slides.heading: From reform to an all-India organisation
slides.body_md: Part 2 — four **reformers** and the founding of the **Indian National Congress**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: four reformers, Raja Rammohan Roy, Jyotiba Phule, Swami Dayananda Saraswati and Swami Vivekananda, and then the founding of the Indian National Congress
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Political grievances were only half the story. Reformers were also changing how Indians saw themselves. In this part we meet four of them, Raja Rammohan Roy, Jyotiba Phule, Swami Dayananda Saraswati and Swami Vivekananda, and then see how, in eighteen eighty-five, nationalists from all over India came together in the Indian National Congress.

slides.heading: Four reformers at a glance
slides.body_md: Each founded an organisation and attacked a different weakness of society.

rows: Against sati (banned 1829); modern education; women's rights
Education of girls and lower castes; against caste discrimination
Return to the Vedas; against caste by birth and child marriage
Chicago address 1893; service to the poor; self-confidence

slides.narration: Here are the four reformers. Raja Rammohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj in eighteen twenty-eight and fought against sati. Jyotiba Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in eighteen seventy-three and worked for girls and the lower castes. Swami Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in eighteen seventy-five. Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission in eighteen ninety-seven.

slides.narration: Raja Rammohan Roy, in Bengal, founded the Brahmo Samaj and campaigned until sati was declared illegal in eighteen twenty-nine. He also supported modern education and the rights of women. Jyotiba Phule, in Maharashtra, opened a school for girls in Pune with his wife Savitribai, and founded the Satyashodhak Samaj to fight discrimination against the lower castes.

questions.stem_md: Indian nationalists of the late nineteenth century used the phrase "drain of wealth". What did it describe?

options.text_md: The loss of water from canals in dry seasons
The transfer of India's wealth to Britain without an equal return to India
The movement of Indian traders to other Asian ports
The money spent by Indian princes on festivals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The transfer of India's wealth to Britain without an equal return to India. The drain meant wealth leaving India for Britain (salaries and pensions of British officials, interest on loans, profits of British firms, home charges) with no matching return. The other options describe unrelated things.

questions.stem_md: Which early nationalist is best known for building the economic argument that British rule was draining India of its wealth?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Dadabhai Naoroji. Dadabhai Naoroji set out the drain argument in his writings, including the book Poverty and Un-British Rule in India. Vivekananda and Phule were reformers; Hume was the founder of the Congress.

questions.stem_md: An imagined British officer retires after thirty years in India and draws his pension in England from Indian revenues. How would an early nationalist classify this payment?

options.text_md: As part of the drain of wealth from India to Britain
As an investment that increased India's income
As a payment made by Britain to India
As a tax paid by the officer to India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** As part of the drain of wealth from India to Britain. Pensions and salaries of British officials paid from Indian revenues and spent in Britain were among the items nationalists counted in the drain. They did not raise India's income, and they flowed from India to Britain, not the reverse.

questions.stem_md: Why did many Indian handloom weavers lose their livelihood in the nineteenth century?

options.text_md: The government banned the growing of cotton in India
Indian weavers were all recruited into the army
Cheap machine-made cloth from British factories flooded Indian markets
Demand for cloth disappeared completely in India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Cheap machine-made cloth from British factories flooded Indian markets. Machine-made British textiles entered India cheaply while Indian goods faced high duties in Britain, so handicrafts declined. Cotton growing was not banned, weavers were not all drafted, and demand for cloth remained.

questions.stem_md: How did the high land-revenue demand of the colonial government add to discontent among peasants?

options.text_md: Peasants received free land from the government every year
Land revenue was abolished, so landlords lost their income
Peasants had to pay heavy revenue even in bad years and often fell into debt to moneylenders
Revenue was collected only from merchants, not from farmers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Peasants had to pay heavy revenue even in bad years and often fell into debt to moneylenders. Heavy and rigid revenue demands pushed peasants into debt and loss of land, which bred resentment. Land was not given free, revenue was not abolished, and it fell mainly on the land.

questions.stem_md: A group of imagined students compares government spending on a grand imperial assembly with relief during the famine of 1876–78. Which nationalist feeling would this comparison most likely have strengthened?

options.text_md: That the government cared more about display than about the suffering of Indians
That famines were caused by the Indian National Congress
That the British government had ended all famines in India
That Indian princes alone were responsible for relief

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** That the government cared more about display than about the suffering of Indians. Holding the Delhi Durbar of 1877 while famine raged was widely seen as indifference to Indian suffering, which nationalists used to criticise British rule. The other options are false or irrelevant.

questions.stem_md: The grand Delhi Durbar of 1877, held while a famine was raging, was organised under which Viceroy?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Lord Lytton. Lord Lytton (Viceroy 1876–80) held the Durbar of 1877 to proclaim Queen Victoria Empress of India. Ripon came after him, Curzon later, and Dalhousie before 1857.

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly describes the Vernacular Press Act of 1878?

options.text_md: It gave all newspapers in India complete freedom
It allowed the government to curb newspapers published in Indian languages, but not English ones
It applied only to English-language newspapers owned by Europeans
It created the first Indian newspaper

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It allowed the government to curb newspapers published in Indian languages, but not English ones. The Act let the government act against Indian-language (vernacular) newspapers that criticised it, while English-language papers were left out, which Indians saw as discrimination. It did not give freedom or target only European papers.

questions.stem_md: Under the Arms Act of 1878, an imagined Indian landowner and an imagined European planter in the same district each want to keep a gun. What does the law require?

options.text_md: The Indian needs a licence, while the European is exempt
Both are exempt from any licence
The European needs a licence, while the Indian is exempt
Neither may ever keep a gun

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Indian needs a licence, while the European is exempt. The Arms Act required Indians to obtain a licence to keep arms, but Europeans and certain officials were exempt, so it was resented as racial discrimination.

questions.stem_md: What did the Ilbert Bill of 1883 propose?

options.text_md: That Europeans could no longer live in India
That Indian judges in the districts could try Europeans in criminal cases
That all judges in India must be British
That newspapers must be licensed every year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** That Indian judges in the districts could try Europeans in criminal cases. Introduced under Lord Ripon, the Bill sought to remove a racial bar so that qualified Indian judges and magistrates could try European offenders. It did not expel Europeans or make all judges British, and it had nothing to do with newspapers.

questions.stem_md: Europeans in India organised a strong protest against the Ilbert Bill and the government gave way. Which lesson did educated Indians most likely draw from this?

options.text_md: The government always ignores public protest
Only armed rebellion could change any law
Organised, united agitation can force the government to change its policy
Indians and Europeans were treated equally in law

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Organised, united agitation can force the government to change its policy. The success of the European agitation showed Indians the power of organised protest and exposed racial inequality, encouraging them to form their own all-India organisation. It disproves the other three statements.

questions.stem_md: Under which Viceroy was the Vernacular Press Act repealed in 1882?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Lord Ripon. Lord Ripon repealed the Act in 1882, 4 years after Lytton had passed it. Canning was Viceroy in 1858 and Minto in the 1900s.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Educated Indians regarded the Vernacular Press Act as discriminatory.

**Reason (R):** The Act targeted newspapers in Indian languages but left English-language newspapers free.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: the different treatment of Indian-language and English papers made the Act look racially unfair.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Delhi Durbar of 1877 angered many Indians.

**Reason (R):** Lord Lytton himself later repealed the Vernacular Press Act.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true: a costly Durbar held while famine raged angered many Indians. R is false: Lytton passed the Act in 1878; it was Lord Ripon who repealed it in 1882.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Arms Act of 1878 applied equally to Indians and Europeans.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Indians needed a licence to keep arms, while Europeans were exempt; the inequality is why the Act was resented.

questions.stem_md: The Vernacular Press Act and the Arms Act were both passed in the year ___ under Lord Lytton.
questions.solution_md: Both Acts were passed in 1878.

questions.stem_md: Mention two channels through which, according to the early nationalists, wealth was drained from India to Britain.
questions.solution_md: Any two channels of the drain.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Salaries and pensions** of British officials paid from Indian revenues and remitted to Britain.
2. **Home charges**, interest on loans and **profits of British firms** sent out of India.

questions.stem_md: How did the decline of Indian handicrafts help the growth of nationalist feeling?
questions.solution_md: Link the economic loss to the nationalist argument.

answer.model_answer_md: Artisans such as weavers **lost their livelihood** to cheap **British machine-made goods** and were pushed onto the land. Nationalists pointed to this **economic ruin** as proof that British rule served **British interests**, which turned economic hardship into **political discontent**.

questions.stem_md: Name any two measures of Lord Lytton that Indians regarded as repressive or insensitive.
questions.solution_md: Any two of the three.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **Vernacular Press Act, 1878**, which curbed Indian-language newspapers.
2. The **Arms Act, 1878**, which required Indians but not Europeans to hold arms licences. (Also: the **Delhi Durbar of 1877** during a famine.)

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why the Ilbert Bill controversy is seen as a step in the growth of Indian nationalism.
questions.solution_md: Racial inequality exposed; lesson of organised agitation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It exposed the **racial attitude** of many Europeans who refused to be tried by Indian judges.
2. The **success of the European agitation** taught Indians the value of **organised, all-India protest**.

questions.stem_md: Explain three ways in which British economic policies created discontent among Indians in the nineteenth century.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct economic causes, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Drain of wealth:** salaries, pensions, interest and profits flowed to Britain without return.
2. **Ruin of handicrafts:** cheap British machine goods destroyed the livelihood of artisans.
3. **Heavy land revenue:** peasants fell into **debt** and lost land, and **famines** found the government slow to help.

questions.stem_md: Which reformer founded the Brahmo Samaj (as the Brahmo Sabha) in 1828?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Raja Rammohan Roy. Raja Rammohan Roy started the Brahmo Sabha, later the Brahmo Samaj, in Calcutta in 1828. Dayananda founded the Arya Samaj, Phule the Satyashodhak Samaj and Vivekananda the Ramakrishna Mission.

questions.stem_md: Raja Rammohan Roy's long campaign helped bring about a regulation of 1829 under Lord William Bentinck. What did it do?

options.text_md: It made English the only language of courts
It set up the first university in India
It declared the practice of sati illegal
It abolished the caste system by law

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It declared the practice of sati illegal. The 1829 regulation banned sati, the burning of widows, after Roy's campaign. The other options are not what the regulation did.

questions.stem_md: An imagined young man in Calcutta in the 1820s wants to study mathematics and science alongside Sanskrit. Which reformer of the time would most strongly have supported his wish?

options.text_md: Lord Lytton, who opposed Indian education
Raja Rammohan Roy, who favoured modern Western education
A. O. Hume, who wanted only English literature taught
No one; modern subjects were unknown in India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Raja Rammohan Roy, who favoured modern Western education. Roy supported the spread of modern, scientific education along with study of Indian traditions. Lytton and Hume do not fit the 1820s, and modern subjects were already being taught in some institutions.

questions.stem_md: Jyotiba Phule founded which organisation in 1873 to work for the rights of the lower castes?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Satyashodhak Samaj. Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (Society of Seekers of Truth) in 1873. The Arya Samaj was Dayananda's, the Prarthana Samaj a Bombay reform society, and the Ramakrishna Mission Vivekananda's.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined history project, students list a reformer who opened a school for girls in Pune with the help of his wife and worked against untouchability. Whom are they describing?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Jyotiba Phule. Jyotiba Phule and Savitribai Phule opened a school for girls in Pune (1848) and worked for the education of girls and lower castes. The others are not linked to this school.

questions.stem_md: In which year did Swami Dayananda Saraswati found the Arya Samaj?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 1875. The Arya Samaj was founded in 1875 (in Bombay). 1828 is the Brahmo Samaj, 1897 the Ramakrishna Mission and 1885 the Congress.

questions.stem_md: Swami Dayananda Saraswati urged Hindus to return to an earlier source of authority as a basis for reform. Which source was it?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Vedas. Dayananda regarded the Vedas as the true source of knowledge and called for a return to them, rejecting later practices such as idol worship and caste by birth. The other sources do not fit his teaching.

questions.stem_md: Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission in which year?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 1897. The Ramakrishna Mission was founded in 1897. Vivekananda spoke at Chicago in 1893; 1875 is the Arya Samaj and 1906 the Muslim League.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student writes: "This reformer's talks at a world gathering of religions in an American city in 1893 made Indians proud of their heritage." Which reformer and city is the student describing?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Swami Vivekananda, Chicago. Vivekananda addressed the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893. Roy died in England in 1833, and Phule and Dayananda did not speak at this gathering.

questions.stem_md: How did the socio-religious reform movements contribute to the rise of nationalism?

options.text_md: They restored self-confidence and pride, and weakened divisions that kept Indians apart
They demanded the immediate end of British rule by force
They were founded by the Indian National Congress
They supported the Vernacular Press Act

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** They restored self-confidence and pride, and weakened divisions that kept Indians apart. By attacking social evils and reviving pride in Indian traditions, the reformers built self-respect and a sense of unity that nationalism drew on. They were not armed movements, they came before the Congress, and they did not support the Press Act.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Ramakrishna Mission ran schools, hospitals and relief work.

**Reason (R):** Swami Vivekananda taught that serving fellow human beings is a way of serving God.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: the Mission's social service grew from Vivekananda's teaching that service to people is service to God.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Swami Dayananda Saraswati opposed caste distinctions based on birth.

**Reason (R):** Swami Dayananda Saraswati founded the Brahmo Samaj.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true: he opposed caste by birth. R is false: he founded the Arya Samaj; the Brahmo Samaj was founded by Raja Rammohan Roy.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Jyotiba Phule founded the Brahmo Samaj in Pune.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873); the Brahmo Samaj was founded by Raja Rammohan Roy in Calcutta (1828).

questions.stem_md: Jyotiba Phule founded the ___ Samaj in 1873.
questions.solution_md: He founded the Satyashodhak Samaj.

questions.stem_md: Match each reformer with the organisation he founded.
questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Roy: Brahmo Samaj; Phule: Satyashodhak Samaj; Dayananda: Arya Samaj; Vivekananda: Ramakrishna Mission.

questions.stem_md: Put the founding of four reform bodies and of the Indian National Congress into the order of their years.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: State two contributions of Raja Rammohan Roy to Indian society.
questions.solution_md: Any two contributions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. He campaigned against **sati**, which was banned in **1829**.
2. He founded the **Brahmo Samaj** (1828) and supported **modern education** and the rights of women.

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which Jyotiba Phule worked for the uplift of the oppressed.
questions.solution_md: Education and the Satyashodhak Samaj.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. With Savitribai Phule, he opened a **school for girls** in Pune and worked for the **education** of girls and lower castes.
2. He founded the **Satyashodhak Samaj (1873)** to fight **caste discrimination**.

questions.stem_md: Mention two ideas or activities of Swami Dayananda Saraswati that encouraged national pride.
questions.solution_md: Any two relevant ideas or activities.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. He called on Indians to return to the **Vedas**, which gave them pride in their own **ancient heritage**.
2. The **Arya Samaj** spread **education** (later through the **DAV schools**) and opposed caste by birth and child marriage.

questions.stem_md: State two contributions of Swami Vivekananda to the awakening of India.
questions.solution_md: Any two contributions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. His address at **Chicago (1893)** won respect for Indian thought abroad and made Indians **proud** of their heritage.
2. He founded the **Ramakrishna Mission (1897)** for **social service** and urged young Indians to be **fearless and self-reliant**.

questions.stem_md: Explain three ways in which the socio-religious reform movements prepared the ground for the national movement.
questions.solution_md: Unity, self-confidence, education.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. They attacked **social evils** such as sati, caste discrimination and child marriage, making society more **united**.
2. They revived **pride** in India's past and built **self-confidence** against claims of Western superiority.
3. They spread **modern education** and a spirit of **enquiry and reason**, producing leaders who later joined the national movement.

questions.stem_md: Which was the most important way in which newspapers helped the growth of nationalism in the late nineteenth century?

options.text_md: They were printed only for British officials
They avoided all discussion of public affairs
They were banned from reporting any news about India
They spread political ideas and criticism of government policies to readers across the country

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** They spread political ideas and criticism of government policies to readers across the country. Newspapers carried political news, debates and criticism of government policy to a wide readership, linking people in different regions. The other options are false.

questions.stem_md: Kesari, a Marathi newspaper started in 1881, is most closely associated with which nationalist?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Bal Gangadhar Tilak. Kesari (Marathi) and Mahratta (English) were associated with Bal Gangadhar Tilak. Surendranath Banerjee ran The Bengalee.

questions.stem_md: The newspaper The Bengalee is associated with which leader?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Surendranath Banerjee. Surendranath Banerjee edited and ran The Bengalee. Naoroji, Phule and Ripon are not linked to it.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Bengali newspaper switches overnight from Bengali to English in 1878. Which new law would it most likely be trying to escape?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Vernacular Press Act. The Vernacular Press Act applied to Indian-language papers only, so a paper printed in English fell outside it. Amrita Bazar Patrika is widely reported to have done exactly this in 1878. The other measures did not concern language.

questions.stem_md: The Hindu, a nationalist English newspaper founded in 1878, was published from which city?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Madras. The Hindu was started in Madras in 1878. Calcutta, Lahore and Allahabad had other papers.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Newspapers helped Indians in different provinces think of common problems.

**Reason (R):** News and opinion about events in one region were read by people in other regions.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: wide circulation of news linked distant regions and built a shared political outlook.

questions.stem_md: True or false? An English-language Indian newspaper in 1879 was outside the scope of the Vernacular Press Act.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The Act covered newspapers in Indian languages, not those in English.

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which the Indian press contributed to the growth of nationalism.
questions.solution_md: Any two roles.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It **criticised government policies**, such as the Press Act and racial laws, and exposed injustice.
2. It spread **political awareness** and carried the ideas of nationalist leaders to people in **many regions**.

questions.stem_md: Name any two nationalist newspapers of the late nineteenth century and the language of each.
questions.solution_md: Any two correctly named with language.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Kesari**, published in **Marathi** and linked with Bal Gangadhar Tilak.
2. **The Hindu**, published in **English** from Madras. (Also acceptable: **Amrita Bazar Patrika**, first Bengali and then English; **The Bengalee**, in English.)

questions.stem_md: Why did the colonial government see the Indian-language press as a threat? Give three reasons.
questions.solution_md: Reach, criticism, shared opinion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Indian-language papers reached **ordinary readers** in towns and villages, not just the English-educated.
2. They **criticised** policies such as the Durbar during famine and the Arms Act, building **public anger**.
3. They created a **shared political opinion** across regions, which could support organised protest.

questions.stem_md: In which year was the Indian National Congress founded?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 1885. The Congress held its first session in December 1885. 1857 is the year of the uprising, 1906 of the Muslim League and 1875 of the Arya Samaj.

questions.stem_md: Which retired British official of the Indian Civil Service is regarded as the founder of the Indian National Congress?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A. O. Hume. Allan Octavian Hume, a retired civil servant, took the lead in founding the Congress. Ripon and Lytton were Viceroys, and Ilbert was the Law Member behind the Ilbert Bill.

questions.stem_md: Where was the first session of the Indian National Congress held?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay. The first session met at the Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay on 28 December 1885 (it had been planned for Poona). The other places were not its venue.

questions.stem_md: Who presided over the first session of the Indian National Congress in 1885?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** W. C. Bonnerjee. Womesh Chunder Bonnerjee presided over the first session. Dadabhai Naoroji presided over the second (Calcutta, 1886).

questions.stem_md: The second session of the Indian National Congress, held in 1886, met in which city and under which President?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Calcutta, under Dadabhai Naoroji. The second session met in Calcutta in 1886 with Dadabhai Naoroji as President. Bombay and Bonnerjee were the first session; Hume was never President of these sessions.

questions.stem_md: About how many delegates attended the first session of the Indian National Congress?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 72. 72 delegates from different parts of India attended the first session in Bombay.

questions.stem_md: Which of these was one of the immediate objectives of the Indian National Congress at its foundation?

options.text_md: To declare complete independence at once
To organise an armed rising against the British
To replace the Viceroy with an Indian ruler in 1886
To bring together nationalists from different regions and promote a feeling of national unity

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** To bring together nationalists from different regions and promote a feeling of national unity. The early Congress aimed to provide a common forum for nationalists, build unity across regions, religions and castes, frame demands and train public opinion. Independence and armed revolt were not its aims in 1885.

questions.stem_md: Some writers described the Congress as a "safety valve" meant to let off Indian discontent harmlessly. Which statement gives a balanced view of this theory?

options.text_md: It is one interpretation; others argue that Indian leaders used Hume's help to build their own national platform
It is the only accepted view, and all historians agree with it
It proves that the Congress was founded by the Viceroy alone
It shows that Indians took no part in founding the Congress

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It is one interpretation; others argue that Indian leaders used Hume's help to build their own national platform. The safety-valve idea is one interpretation of Hume's motives; many historians stress that Indian leaders, who were already forming associations, used his help to found an all-India body. The other options overstate or misstate the case.

questions.stem_md: An imagined lawyer in Calcutta in 1880 belongs to a political association founded by Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose. Which association is it?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Indian Association. The Indian Association (1876) of Calcutta was one of the regional bodies that came before the Congress. The Muslim League (1906) and Forward Bloc (1939) came later, and the Satyashodhak Samaj was a social reform body.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The first session of the Congress was attended by delegates from different provinces.

**Reason (R):** A. O. Hume was a retired member of the Indian Civil Service.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but R does not explain A: the all-India attendance reflected the aim of national unity and earlier regional associations, not Hume's former service.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At its first session in 1885 the Congress demanded complete independence from Britain.

**Reason (R):** The early Congress worked through petitions and resolutions placed before the government.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: the 1885 Congress sought reforms and a greater share for Indians, not complete independence. R is true: its early method was petitions, prayers and resolutions.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Dadabhai Naoroji presided over the first session of the Indian National Congress.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. W. C. Bonnerjee presided over the first session (1885); Naoroji presided over the second (1886).

questions.stem_md: The first session of the Indian National Congress was presided over by W. C. ___.
questions.solution_md: W. C. Bonnerjee presided.

questions.stem_md: The first session of the Indian National Congress began in Bombay on 28 ___ 1885.
questions.solution_md: It began on 28 December 1885.

questions.stem_md: Mention two immediate objectives of the Indian National Congress at the time of its foundation.
questions.solution_md: Any two objectives.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. To provide a **common platform** where nationalists from all parts of India could meet and work together.
2. To promote **national unity** across region, religion and caste, and to **formulate demands** to place before the government.

questions.stem_md: Name the Presidents and venues of the first two sessions of the Indian National Congress.
questions.solution_md: Two sessions, each with venue and President.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **first session** met in **Bombay in 1885**, with **W. C. Bonnerjee** as President.
2. The **second session** met in **Calcutta in 1886**, with **Dadabhai Naoroji** as President.

questions.stem_md: Give one view of why A. O. Hume helped found the Congress, and one reason why Indian leaders welcomed his help.
questions.solution_md: One interpretation of Hume's motive; one reason for Indian acceptance.

answer.model_answer_md:
**View:** some writers argue he wanted a **safety valve** for rising discontent; others see it as genuine **sympathy** for Indian demands.
**Indian leaders:** a retired British official at the head made the new body **less suspect** to the government, helping it **survive** in its early years.

questions.stem_md: Why did educated Indians feel the need for an all-India political organisation by the 1880s? Give three reasons.
questions.solution_md: Limits of regional bodies; lesson of organised protest; common grievances.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Regional associations** (such as the Indian Association) had shown the value of organisation but were limited to one area.
2. Events like the **Ilbert Bill** controversy showed that **united, organised** protest could succeed.
3. Common grievances (**drain, Press Act, Arms Act**) affected Indians everywhere and needed a **national voice**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the economic causes of Indian nationalism.

(i) What did the early nationalists mean by the "drain of wealth"? **[3]**
(ii) How did British policy lead to the decline of Indian handicrafts? **[3]**
(iii) Explain how the condition of peasants and the experience of famines added to Indian discontent. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Drain; ruin of crafts; peasants and famines.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Wealth flowed from India to **Britain** without an equal return: **salaries and pensions** of British officials, **home charges**, **interest** on loans and **profits** of British firms. **Dadabhai Naoroji** set out this argument in detail.

(ii) Cheap **machine-made British goods** entered India freely, while Indian goods faced high **duties** in Britain; Indian crafts lost both foreign and home markets, and many **artisans** lost their livelihood and turned to agriculture.

(iii) A **heavy land-revenue** demand had to be paid even in bad years, so peasants fell into **debt** to moneylenders and lost land. During **famines** such as that of **1876–78**, relief seemed inadequate, and holding the **Delhi Durbar of 1877** at the same time convinced many that the government cared little for Indian lives.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about colonial policies that angered Indians.

(i) Explain the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 and why Indians objected to it. **[3]**
(ii) Explain the Arms Act of 1878 and its effect on Indian opinion. **[3]**
(iii) What was the Ilbert Bill controversy, and how did it influence the growth of nationalism? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Press Act; Arms Act; Ilbert Bill.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Passed under **Lord Lytton**, it allowed the government to act against **Indian-language** newspapers that criticised it, while **English** papers were left free. Indians saw it as an attack on **free expression** and as **discrimination**.

(ii) It required **Indians** to hold a **licence** to keep arms, while **Europeans** were **exempt**. Indians felt **humiliated** and saw it as proof of **racial inequality**.

(iii) Under **Lord Ripon (1883)**, the Bill proposed that **Indian judges** could try **Europeans** in criminal cases. Europeans protested strongly and the government **compromised**. Indians saw the **racial attitude** behind the protest and learnt that **organised agitation** works, which encouraged the formation of an **all-India organisation**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about two social reformers.

(i) State the contributions of Raja Rammohan Roy. **[3]**
(ii) State the contributions of Jyotiba Phule. **[3]**
(iii) How did the work of these two reformers help create national consciousness? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Roy; Phule; link to national consciousness.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) He founded the **Brahmo Samaj (1828)**, campaigned against **sati** (banned in **1829**), and supported **modern education** and the rights of **women**, including property rights.

(ii) With **Savitribai Phule** he opened a **school for girls** in Pune and worked for the education of the **lower castes**; he founded the **Satyashodhak Samaj (1873)** to fight **caste** discrimination.

(iii) By attacking **social evils** they made society more **just and united**; they spread **education** and a spirit of **reason**; and by restoring **self-respect** to women and the oppressed, they widened the circle of people who would later join the **national movement**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about two religious reformers.

(i) What were the main ideas of Swami Dayananda Saraswati and the Arya Samaj? **[3]**
(ii) What were the contributions of Swami Vivekananda? **[3]**
(iii) Compare the ways in which these two reformers built pride and self-confidence among Indians. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Dayananda; Vivekananda; comparison.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) He founded the **Arya Samaj (1875)**, called for a return to the **Vedas**, opposed **idol worship**, **caste by birth** and **child marriage**, and supported **education** (later the **DAV** schools).

(ii) A disciple of **Ramakrishna Paramahansa**, he spoke at the **World's Parliament of Religions, Chicago (1893)**, founded the **Ramakrishna Mission (1897)** for **social service**, and urged young Indians to be **strong and fearless**.

(iii) **Dayananda** built pride by turning Indians towards their **ancient Vedic heritage** and reforming society from within. **Vivekananda** built confidence by winning **respect abroad** for Indian thought and by linking **religion with service** to the poor. Both rejected the idea that Indians were **inferior**, which strengthened national feeling.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Kesari** (Marathi) – **Bal Gangadhar Tilak**; **The Bengalee** – **Surendranath Banerjee**; **The Hindu** – **Madras** (also **Amrita Bazar Patrika**, Calcutta).

(ii) It **criticised** unjust policies; it spread **political awareness** and the ideas of leaders; it **linked regions** so that people saw common problems and a common cause.

(iii) The government feared the growing influence of **Indian-language** papers, which reached ordinary readers and criticised measures such as the **Durbar** and the **Arms Act**; **Lytton** passed the Act in **1878**. questions.solution_md: Foundation; objectives; first two sessions.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) It was founded on **28 December 1885** at the **Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay**; **A. O. Hume**, a retired member of the Indian Civil Service, took the lead.

(ii) To provide a **common platform** for nationalists from all parts of India; to promote **national unity** across region, religion and caste; to **formulate demands** and place them before the government; and to **train public opinion** (any three).

(iii) **First session, Bombay, 1885:** presided over by **W. C. Bonnerjee**, attended by **72 delegates**. **Second session, Calcutta, 1886:** presided over by **Dadabhai Naoroji**, with a much larger attendance.

questions.stem_md:
Historians have long discussed why the Congress came into being in 1885.

(i) Explain three developments of the 1870s and 1880s that made an all-India organisation necessary. **[3]**
(ii) What is the "safety-valve" theory of the Congress's origin? **[3]**
(iii) Present one argument that supports and one argument that questions the safety-valve theory, and state which you find more convincing. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Developments; meaning of the theory; balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Repressive measures** of Lytton (Press Act, Arms Act) gave Indians common grievances; the **Ilbert Bill** controversy showed the power of organised protest; **regional associations** such as the **Indian Association (1876)** had shown the value of organisation but needed a national body.

(ii) It is the view that **Hume** wanted the Congress as a **safety valve**, a channel through which growing **discontent** could be let out **peacefully**, so that it would not turn into a violent outbreak like **1857**.

(iii) **Supports:** Hume was a former **official** who worried about unrest, and the early Congress was **moderate** and loyal in tone. **Questions:** Indian leaders were **already organising** and **used** Hume's help to gain a **legitimate national platform**; the Congress soon became a **vehicle of nationalism**. A balanced answer may find the second more convincing because the Congress grew far beyond any safety-valve purpose; either view earns credit if reasoned.
